name: Chloe Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Chloe Ito, forty-three, and I drive a haul truck at the large mine outside town. I do the walk-round before dawn, carry rock from the pit to the crusher, and spend most of the shift watching mirrors and tyre warnings. I'm still junior, so I ask the older drivers when a sound seems wrong. The regular wage keeps our mortgage paid, but with two children in school and less than a month's bills saved, a missed shift lands hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the truck still needs a person watching the road and the load. I'd say a little screen automation might tidy our reports, but it won't settle the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I privately worry about short shifts already, because the mine has sent us home when the conveyor stops. My partner's shop hours vary, and our savings would not cover a full month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking assigned shifts and checking the haul truck before each run. I'd put any overtime pay straight against the small credit card balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel tired more than frightened by the AI part. The ordinary worry is whether the next pay packet will cover the school shoes and the mortgage in the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when a shift is cancelled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the conveyor stopped and I lost one Saturday. I delayed buying new trainers for my son until the following pay day; he managed, but I hated making him wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell someone who says the mine is secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the pit can be busy and still send a junior driver home first. The truck is there, but my name isn't guaranteed on every roster.

do: Keep taking **assigned shifts** and checking the haul truck before each run.
Put any **overtime pay** straight against the small credit card balance.
feel: **Tired** by ordinary costs even if AI barely changes the mine.
**Worried** that school shoes and the mortgage land in one pay week.
S0.quote: I'd say the pit can be busy and still send a junior driver home first.
fieldNote: **Thin savings** make even unchanged mine work feel fragile when a shift disappears.
She speaks confidently about the truck but counts **household purchases** by pay day, revealing how narrow her margin is.

steps.text: Keep driving assigned haul truck shifts and checking tyres before runs
Pay overtime earnings against the credit card balance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues office tasks will change first, while someone still has to steer a loaded truck. I'd ask the supervisor whether rosters will shrink before telling my family everything is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think automated dispatch could leave fewer drivers waiting when production slows. I'm not quick with new screens, and junior drivers are easier to leave off a roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the shift supervisor which dispatch tasks are changing this month. I'd keep driving my haul runs and set aside overtime before buying anything extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me uneasy in my stomach even though the robots arrive slowly in this picture. The mine can save money in the control room before anyone touches my truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your supervisor exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether a new dispatch system means fewer haul trucks on the morning roster. I wouldn't pretend I can learn a new console in one afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply elsewhere if that roster fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first ask for a different shift at this mine. There are few other mines nearby, and moving both schoolchildren for a rumour would be a large gamble.

S1.quote: The mine can save money in the control room before anyone touches my truck.
fieldNote: She expects **dispatch changes** before driver replacement, but fears fewer available shifts at her junior standing.
Her first response is a **supervisor question** and tighter spending; she avoids promising a move she cannot afford.

steps.text: Ask the shift supervisor whether dispatch software will reduce morning haul runs
Keep taking scheduled truck runs while dispatch changes are tested
Set aside overtime instead of buying extra household items

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI in 2028 changes the office before it changes the pit. I'd say robots in 2031 put truck jobs at risk, and the company owes drivers a straight answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-five in 2028, I might still be driving, but paperwork and dispatch could be handled elsewhere. At forty-eight when the robots arrive, I expect the junior drivers to lose paid runs first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union representative for a meeting about driver jobs and retraining terms now. I'd keep taking paid truck shifts through 2028 while cutting our takeaway meals. I'd apply for maintenance assistant openings at the mine if driver runs fall in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel scared enough to wake before the alarm. A truck can't become autonomous just because an office program is clever. Three years is a short breath when our mortgage lasts much longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes at home this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the Friday takeaway and put that money toward the mortgage arrears buffer. I would tell the children the family is saving for a dull reason, not make them carry my fear about the pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance if you are still learning to drive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the inspection routine and can spot a bad tyre, but I'd need someone to train me properly. I'd apply for an assistant opening if the driver roster fell, even if the first wage was smaller.

I'd say robots in **2031** put truck jobs at risk, and the company owes drivers a straight answer.

At forty-eight when the **robots** arrive, I expect the junior drivers to lose paid runs first.

Apply for **maintenance assistant** openings at the mine if driver runs fall in 2031.

**Pressed** by a robot date much earlier than the mortgage end.
S2.quote: Three years is a short breath when our mortgage lasts much longer.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 office change** from 2031 robot replacement and expects her junior truck hours to disappear then.
Her plan combines **union questions**, continued wages, smaller household spending and conditional applications for mine maintenance work.

steps.text: Ask the union representative about driver jobs and funded maintenance training
Keep taking paid haul truck shifts through the 2028 change
Stop Friday takeaways and direct the money toward a mortgage buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my workmates five years gives us more notice but no right to assume the trucks stay human-driven. I'd press for the mine to publish a driver plan before people sign new loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be forty-eight when thinking AI arrives, and most of my day will still be in the cab. At fifty-one in 2034, I expect robot haulage to put my own wage in danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union to request a driver timeline from management this year. I'd enroll in a maintenance certificate if the mine funds places and releases me from shifts. I'd keep earning on the truck and pay down the credit card before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me room to breathe, though I don't mistake room for a guarantee. I could learn a repair task slowly if a real instructor stood beside me; a screen-only course would defeat me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need paid time and a workshop instructor, not an unpaid course after a twelve-hour shift. My secondary school education is enough for the work I do now, but I need patient practice for a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mine does not fund it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the truck wage while it lasts and ask the union what other sites have arranged. I couldn't pay course fees upfront with less than one month's expenses saved.

feel: **Relieved** to have a few more years of warning.
**Alarmed** that robot haulage could still remove her wage.
S3.quote: I couldn't pay course fees upfront with less than one month's expenses saved.
fieldNote: She sees the **2034 robot date** as the point her own wage may fail, despite a longer warning period.
**Training** is a real option only with funded places and paid release; she does not claim a certificate already exists.

steps.text: Ask the union to request a published driver timeline from mine management
Enroll in mine funded maintenance training if paid release is offered
Keep driving paid haul truck shifts while places are arranged
Pay down the credit card with overtime before robot haulage arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to plan, but the robot trucks in 2039 still matter to the drivers. I'd tell the crew I want plain dates rather than another glossy mine presentation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three when thinking AI arrives, I may have older children but still owe on the house. At fifty-six when robots arrive, I cannot assume retirement or a pension will replace my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working truck shifts while asking management for its long-term equipment timetable. I'd pay extra toward the mortgage only when overtime leaves enough for a month's bills. I'd enroll in a workshop course if funded places open before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade feels less like a shove and more like a road with turns. I still dislike learning from a machine, but I can handle a real teacher showing me one job at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the children be placed by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be grown by 2036, so school costs should ease, but I won't count their wages as mine. I would still need to keep the mortgage current and work for my own living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire when robot trucks come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, fifty-six is too early for me to promise retirement, and I don't know what pension I'll have. I'd rather have workshop skills and an actual job application in hand if haulage shrinks.

I'd tell the crew I want **plain dates** rather than another glossy mine presentation.
think: At fifty-three when **thinking AI** arrives, I may have older children but still owe on the house.
At fifty-six when **robots** arrive, I cannot assume retirement or a pension will replace my pay.

**Anxious** about paid work at fifty-six without a known pension.
S4.quote: I would still need to keep the mortgage current and work for my own living.
fieldNote: The longer runway softens her fear, while **mortgage payments** and uncertain retirement income remain central.

steps.text: Keep driving scheduled haul truck shifts while asking for equipment dates

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robot haulage could reach my truck before I can learn another paid job. A published driver timetable, paid workshop training, and enough notice to apply for openings at the mine would help me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who covers the children when a training course runs after school. My partner works changing shop hours, so a course has to fit a real family timetable or I won't finish it.

headlineQuote: The truck is there, but my name isn't guaranteed on every roster.
portrait: Chloe is a **junior haul driver** at a large mine, with two school-age children and a mortgage.
Less than a month's **savings** makes lost shifts painful even under AI Plateau.
She expects thinking AI to alter **dispatch** before robots threaten her truck work about three years later.
She prefers paid, instructor-led **maintenance training** and resists making plans around unconfirmed mine promises.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves her too little time to prepare for robot haulage around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A published **driver timetable** and paid workshop training would let her apply for other mine work.
Training must fit **childcare hours** because her partner's shop shifts change.
